model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about one app that I am using every day. It is a transport app and it shows the bus times.

So it is very simple. You open it and you can see when the bus is coming. It is very useful because sometimes the bus is late and you don't know. So this app tells you.

I found this app from my colleague. One day we were at the bus stop and it was raining, and she was looking at her phone. So I asked her and she told me the name. And after that I downloaded it in the same evening.

I use it in the morning before I go out. And also I use it when I come back from work. Sometimes at the weekend also, if I go to a new place.

Why I keep using it. Because it is very easy and very fast. I tried another app before, a big one, but it has too many things inside and it was slow. So I deleted it. This app is more better for me because it is simple. So yes, this is the app that I use every day and I think it is very good.

what_caps_it.point: Almost every sentence opens with 'so' or 'and', so nothing is subordinated.
'Very useful', 'very easy', 'very fast', 'very good' — one adjective pattern doing all the work.
'Am using' for a habit, 'more better', and a present tense inside a past story.

annotations.span: I found this app from my colleague.
annotations.label: Answers the bullet directly
annotations.why: Keep this habit — name the source in one sentence before you add detail.

annotations.span: one app that I am using every day
annotations.label: Continuous used for a habit
annotations.why: Regular habits take the present simple: 'an app I use every day'.

annotations.span: but it has too many things inside and it was slow
annotations.label: Tense slips mid-sentence
annotations.why: You started in the past — keep 'had' and 'was' together.

annotations.span: This app is more better for me
annotations.label: Double comparative
annotations.why: Say 'better'. Never put 'more' in front of an -er form.

annotations.span: I think it is very good
annotations.label: Flat closing evaluation
annotations.why: Close on what it changes for you, not on 'good'.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The one I'd pick is a small transport app that shows live bus times — nothing clever, it simply tells you where the bus actually is rather than where the timetable claims it should be. It opens on a single screen and there's no account to sign into, which is half the appeal.

I came across it completely by accident. I was standing at a stop one evening and a colleague had it open at the stop while we were both getting soaked, and I remember thinking it was slightly absurd that I'd been using that route for years without knowing such a thing existed. I installed it the same night and I've stuck with it ever since.

As for when I use it, it's mainly first thing in the morning, before I've even put my coat on, because it saves me standing outside for eleven minutes in February. I check it again on the way home, and occasionally at weekends if I'm going somewhere I don't know.

Why I've kept it rather than switching — I suppose it's that it does one thing well. I did try one of the big all-in-one travel apps, and it was crammed with features I'd never touch, whereas this one opens straight onto the stop nearest me. It also loads fast, which sounds trivial until you're doing it in the rain with cold hands. Honestly, the test for me with anything on my phone is whether I'd notice it going, and I'd notice this one within a day.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Crammed with features', 'does one thing well', 'half the appeal' replace the flat adjectives.
A past perfect, a contrastive 'whereas' clause and a clean present perfect for duration.
Each bullet is announced, so the listener always knows which part is running.

annotations.label: Opens with a choice, not a preamble
annotations.why: Naming the subject in four words leaves the rest of the ten seconds for detail.

annotations.span: rather than where the timetable claims it should be
annotations.label: Contrast built into the description
annotations.why: Defining a thing against what it is not is quicker than listing features.

annotations.span: I'd been using that route for years without knowing such a thing existed
annotations.label: Past perfect continuous for backstory
annotations.why: Use it once to show the situation before the moment you are describing.

annotations.span: I've stuck with it ever since
annotations.label: Present perfect for duration
annotations.why: 'Ever since' plus present perfect is the natural close to a discovery story.

annotations.span: As for when I use it
annotations.label: Signposts the third bullet
annotations.why: Saying which bullet you are on stops you skipping one under pressure.

annotations.span: it was crammed with features I'd never touch, whereas this one opens straight onto the stop nearest me
annotations.label: Comparison joined with 'whereas'
annotations.why: 'Whereas' links two full clauses and does the evaluating for you.

annotations.span: which sounds trivial until you're doing it in the rain with cold hands
annotations.label: Concedes then justifies
annotations.why: Admitting a point is small, then showing when it isn't, reads as real thinking.

annotations.span: the test for me with anything on my phone is whether I'd notice it going
annotations.label: Stress lands on 'notice'
annotations.why: Put the emphasis on the word carrying the idea, not on the last word.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The app I'd single out is an unglamorous little thing that tracks live bus times — it doesn't plan your journey or sell you anything, it just tells you where the bus has actually got to. One screen, no login, and it has quietly become part of leaving the house.

I stumbled on it years ago in the least romantic circumstances imaginable: a colleague had it open at a stop in the rain while the two of us stood there guessing. What struck me wasn't the app so much as how long I'd put up with not knowing. I had it installed before I got home.

These days I check it before I've got my coat on, again somewhere around six, and at weekends if I'm heading anywhere unfamiliar. It's become entirely automatic — I couldn't tell you when I last decided to open it. It's the sort of habit you only notice yourself having when somebody asks you about it.

As for why it survived and its rivals didn't, I think it's simply that it knows what it isn't. The all-in-one travel apps I tried were stuffed with things I'd never use, and every extra feature bought a fraction of a second of loading time. Rarely does a piece of software win by doing less, but this one does. And that, I suspect, is the real test of anything you use daily — not whether it impresses you, but whether you'd notice the hole it left.

what_lifts_it.point: Negative inversion with 'rarely does', plus a cleft that band 7 stated plainly.
'Stumbled on', 'put up with', 'stuffed with' sit naturally instead of being displayed.
The close generalises about software rather than summarising the answer.

annotations.span: Rarely does a piece of software win by doing less
annotations.label: Negative inversion
annotations.why: Front a negative adverb and invert. One per turn is plenty.

annotations.span: I stumbled on it years ago in the least romantic circumstances imaginable
annotations.label: Idiom plus a dry judgement
annotations.why: Two natural idioms in two minutes beat five decorative ones.

annotations.span: how long I'd put up with not knowing
annotations.label: Phrasal verb doing precise work
annotations.why: 'Put up with' says tolerated-reluctantly in three ordinary words.

annotations.span: it knows what it isn't
annotations.label: A judgement compressed into five words
annotations.why: Short sentences after long ones make the point land.

annotations.span: not whether it impresses you, but whether you'd notice the hole it left
annotations.label: Balanced pair, falling at the end
annotations.why: Keep the pitch level across 'impresses you', then drop on 'left'.

model_answers.transcript:
The one that comes to mind is a documentary about the people who clean office buildings at night. It isn't dramatic in the slightest — there's no narrator and no music, it simply follows one crew through a single shift, from about ten in the evening until five, and lets them talk while they work.

I came to it more or less by accident. I couldn't sleep, it was on late, and I only meant to give it ten minutes. In the end I sat through the whole thing with the sound turned right down so I wouldn't wake anybody up, which is not how I usually watch anything.

I was on my own, and I think that mattered — there was nobody there to make a joke and break the spell. I did talk about it the next day with my sister, who works in a hospital, and she said it was exactly the same on her wards: an entire shift of people the daytime staff essentially never meet.

As for what it changed — it changed who I notice. Before that I'd have walked straight past the man mopping the lobby without registering him at all, not out of rudeness, but because the whole arrangement is designed to keep that work out of sight. Now I catch myself wondering when a place was cleaned, and by whom, which sounds like a small thing until you realise it applies to nearly everything you use. And the programme never says any of that. It films people doing their jobs and lets you get there yourself.

The programme I keep coming back to is a documentary about night cleaners in office blocks. It has almost nothing in the way of technique — no narration, no score, no arc to speak of. It follows one crew from ten at night until five in the morning and simply refuses to look away.

I found it by accident, in the way you find most things at one in the morning. I gave it ten minutes out of politeness to nobody in particular and ended up watching the lot with the volume at a whisper.

I watched it alone, which I now think was the point. There was no one to lighten it with a comment. What I did do was ring my sister the following day — she's a nurse — and she was entirely unsurprised: on her wards there is a whole population of staff the day shift never lays eyes on.

What changed wasn't my opinion of anything, it was my attention. Never had it occurred to me to wonder who cleans the building I work in, and that isn't carelessness so much as design: the work is scheduled precisely so that nobody has to see it. That, I think, is what the better documentaries do. They don't hand you an argument. They rearrange what you happen to notice, and the argument arrives on its own about a week later, by which point it feels like something you worked out yourself.

I will describe one account that I am following on social media. It is about the history of my city.

Every morning they are posting one old photo of the city. And under the photo there is small text, two lines, where it is and which year. I think one man is doing it, a teacher, but I am not sure.

I follow it since three years. My cousin shared one photo and then I saw it, and after that I clicked follow.

The photos are different. Sometimes it is a street, sometimes a shop or a bus. Some of them I know the place and some I don't know. And many people are writing comments under it, and they are discussing which street it is.

model_answers.transcript:
The one I'd talk about is a local history account that posts one old photograph of my city every morning, with two or three lines underneath saying roughly where it was taken and when. It's run by a retired teacher, as far as I can tell, working entirely on his own and with no apparent interest in being noticed.

I've been following it for about three years now. It turned up in my feed because a cousin had shared one of the pictures, and I stayed as much for the comments as for the photographs — half the city seems to appear underneath, arguing about which street it actually is.

What it posts is quite narrow, and that's the appeal. One picture, one caption, no opinion about anything. Some mornings it's a tram on a road that doesn't exist any more; other mornings it's a shopfront that has since become a phone repair shop. Every so often he'll put the modern view beside it, and that's when the comments really take off.

As for why I've kept it when I've cleared out almost everything else — I think it's because it asks nothing of me. There's no outrage in it, nothing is trying to sell me a course, and the whole thing takes about eleven seconds. It's also taught me a fair amount about the place I live in, which I certainly hadn't signed up for. If more of what I followed behaved like that, I'd spend a lot less time wishing I were off my phone.

The account I'd pick is a quiet local history page that puts up a single archive photograph of my city each morning, captioned with a street name and an approximate year. It appears to be one retired teacher, working alone, with no interest whatsoever in growing.

I've had it in my feed for three years or so. A cousin shared one of the pictures, I followed on impulse, and unlike almost everything else I acquired that year it survived. What kept me there initially wasn't the photographs at all but the argument underneath them: half the city turns up to insist that the corner in question is not the corner he says it is.

The format never varies. One image, two lines, no commentary. A tram on a street that was flattened decades ago; a bakery that is now a phone repair shop. Nothing is ever explained and nothing is ever argued for. Occasionally he sets the modern view alongside, at which point the comments become genuinely heated.

What has kept it, when I've stripped out practically everything else, is that it wants nothing from me. No outrage, no course to buy, eleven seconds and gone. I look at it before I'm properly awake and I have never once resented it. And it has taught me more about this city than I ever set out to learn, which I suspect is the only way anybody learns anything now — sideways, from something they were only half looking at.

I want to talk about one time when I saw something on the internet and it was not true.

It was a message in our family group. The message says that one food can stop a very serious illness, and there is a photo of a laboratory, so it looks very official. My aunt sent it. She is not a stupid person, but she believed it.

And many people in the group answered, thank you, this is very useful. So I also thought maybe it is true.

But then I read it again and something is strange. It writes the name of a university. So I searched this university and I found the study. And the study is real, but it is about a different thing completely. The number in the message is from another place.

After that I was thinking what to do. If I write in the group, my aunt will feel bad in front of everybody. So I sent her a private message and I sent the study, and I said I also almost believed it. This happened a couple of years ago, in one of those family groups on a messaging app that you can never quite leave. Somebody had forwarded a message claiming that a particular food could prevent a fairly serious illness, with a photograph of a laboratory attached to make it look official.

It reached us through my aunt, who is not a foolish woman at all. She'd been sent it by a friend, who'd been sent it by somebody else, and by the time it arrived nobody had any idea where it had started. Three or four relatives had already replied saying how useful it was, so my first instinct, honestly, was to assume it was fine.

What made me look properly was the wording. It named a university, so I searched for the study — and the study did exist. It simply didn't say anything remotely like what the message claimed. It was about something else entirely, and the figure it quoted had been lifted from a completely different table.

As for what I did, that's the part I still think about. I didn't correct it in the group, because I could see exactly how that would go: my aunt would have been shown up in front of everybody and she'd have dug her heels in. So I messaged her privately, sent her the actual paper, and told her I'd nearly believed it myself, which was true. She deleted it an hour later without being asked. Looking back, if I'd said it publicly I'm fairly sure that message would still be circulating.

This was two or three years back, in one of those family groups nobody has the nerve to leave. A message had been forwarded round claiming that a particular food headed off a fairly serious illness, and it came with a stock photograph of a laboratory, which is apparently all it takes.

It reached me through an aunt of mine — a sharp woman, not remotely gullible. She'd had it from a friend, who'd had it from somebody else, and its origins had long since vanished. Several relatives had already thanked her for it, and I'll admit my own first reaction was to let it go.

What snagged on me was the wording. It named a university, so I went looking, and the paper turned out to be perfectly real — it simply had nothing to do with the claim. Different subject, different question, and the figure in the message had been quietly borrowed from an unrelated table.

Then came the awkward part. Had I posted the correction in the group, my aunt would have been humiliated in front of thirty relatives and would have defended it to the last. So I went to her privately, sent the paper, and said I'd very nearly fallen for it myself — which happened to be true. She took it down within the hour. What I took from that is that being right is only half of it; the other half is leaving somebody a way to change their mind.

I want to tell about the time when I repaired a tap in my kitchen. It was dripping for many weeks and it was very annoying because I can hear it from the other room.

So I decided to repair it myself. I don't want to pay a plumber for such a small thing. I searched on the internet and I found a video. In the video there is a man in a garage and he does everything in four minutes. Also there was a text guide from a shop but I only looked it quickly.

The repair is not difficult. You remove the handle, you open the top, you change one small rubber piece and you close everything. But the problem is I don't stop the water first. The man says it in the beginning but I jumped this part because I want to see the important part.

So when I opened the top, all the water came on my face. It was very shocking. And after that I was searching the valve on the floor for five minutes.

model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about the time I tried to fix a dripping tap in my kitchen. It had been going for weeks and had reached the stage where I could hear it from the next room, so it was that or lose my mind.

The instructions came from a video, inevitably. I'd searched for the make of the tap and found a man in a garage who got through the whole job in about four minutes, with the camera propped on a paint tin. There was a written guide on a hardware shop's site as well, which I skim-read and, in hindsight, should have read properly.

How it went is the interesting part. The repair itself is straightforward: you take the handle off, unscrew the top, replace a small rubber washer, and put it all back. What I hadn't done was turn the water off at the mains, because the video mentions it in the first fifteen seconds and I'd skipped ahead to the section that looked useful. So the moment I loosened the top I got a face full of cold water, and spent the next five minutes on the kitchen floor hunting for a valve I'd never once thought about.

What I'd do differently is embarrassingly obvious — watch the whole thing before touching anything. Although I'd also say the panic taught me more than the video did. If it had gone smoothly I'd have forgotten it by the weekend, whereas I now know exactly where that valve is, and I've fixed two more since.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The occasion I'd pick is the afternoon I decided to deal with a tap in my kitchen that had been dripping since roughly the previous autumn and had got audible from two rooms away.

My instructions came, as everybody's now do, from a video: a man in a garage, camera balanced on a paint tin, the entire job dispatched in four minutes flat. There was a written version on a hardware chain's site as well, which I skimmed in the way one skims a safety card on an aeroplane.

The job itself could hardly be simpler. Handle off, top unscrewed, a rubber washer the size of a coin swapped out, everything back. What I had failed to do — and it is mentioned inside the first fifteen seconds, which tells you how far I'd skipped ahead — was turn the water off at the mains. Loosening that top produced a jet of cold water straight into my face and five undignified minutes crawling about looking for a valve whose existence had never crossed my mind.

What would I change? Watch the thing through, obviously. But had it gone to plan, I'd have forgotten the whole business by Sunday. As it is, I could find that valve in the dark, and I've since done two more taps without incident. There's a case for saying that nothing you get right first time ever really sticks, and that the useful part of any instruction is the step you were too impatient to watch.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I will talk about the thing that I do for keeping contact with my friend. Every Sunday I am sending her a long voice message, and she sends me one back on Monday usually.

She is my friend from the university. She moved to another country six years ago. There is five hours difference between us, so it is not easy.

In the beginning we are trying to call. But it was always a problem. When I am free she is sleeping, and when she is free I am working. And also when we finally called, we prepared many things to say in the week, and then we said nothing. It was strange.

So after that we started the voice messages. They are very long, maybe ten minutes, and they are about nothing important. What she ate, some problem in her office, a book. I record mine when I walk home so there is a lot of noise.

Why this one continues. Because there is no appointment. Nobody must be free in one exact time, so nobody feels bad. And I think now I know her daily life more than before, when we lived in the same city. So it is a very nice habit.

what_caps_it.point: Continuous forms used for habits throughout, and 'since'-style duration never appears.
'Not easy', 'strange', 'nice', 'important' — the whole judgement rests on four flat words.
'So' and 'and' open six sentences, so the reasoning is stated but never subordinated.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The thing I'd describe isn't remotely impressive: I send a long voice message to a friend of mine every Sunday evening, and she sends one back, usually on the Monday.

We were at university together and she moved abroad about six years ago, which put five hours between us. We tried calling for a while and it was hopeless — either I was at work or she was asleep, and on the rare occasions we managed it we'd both spent the whole week storing things up and then said none of them.

So at some point we gave up on calls altogether. The messages are about ten minutes long, which sounds excessive, and they're almost entirely about nothing: what she had for lunch, an argument with a colleague, whatever she happens to be reading. I record mine walking home, so there's traffic all over the recording, and neither of us edits anything or, as far as I know, ever listens back to their own.

As for why this one has lasted when every other habit I started that year has fallen by the wayside — I think it's because there's no arrangement to break. Nobody has to be free at a particular hour, nobody feels guilty for missing one, and if I'm honest it's easier to say something real into a phone than across a video call where you spend the time watching your own face. Six years on, I probably know more about her ordinary week than I ever did in the two years we lived in the same building.

what_lifts_it.point: Frequency adverbs land correctly, and 'we'd spent … and then said' holds one past frame.
'Storing things up', 'fallen by the wayside', 'no arrangement to break' carry the meaning.
The reason bullet is the longest section, and it gives a mechanism rather than a feeling.

annotations.label: Distance expressed as time
annotations.why: Six words replace a whole clause about time zones.

annotations.label: Frequency inside a noun phrase
annotations.why: 'On the rare occasions' is more precise than 'sometimes' and sounds spoken.

annotations.label: Past perfect then past simple
annotations.why: Two layers of past in one sentence, with no dates required.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
What I do is almost aggressively unremarkable. Every Sunday evening I record a rambling voice message for a friend from university, and one arrives back from her, generally on the Monday.

She went abroad six years ago, which put five hours and a working week between us. We persevered with calls for a while and they were a disaster: whenever I was free she was asleep, and the handful we did manage had the peculiar quality of two people who had saved up a fortnight of news and then couldn't think of a word of it.

So the calls quietly stopped. What replaced them runs to about ten minutes a side and concerns nothing whatsoever — lunch, a colleague who has annoyed her, three pages of a book. Mine are recorded walking home, traffic and all. Neither of us has ever edited one, and I doubt either of us listens back.

What has kept it alive, when every other habit from that year fell by the wayside, is precisely that there is nothing to break. No hour to be free at, no apology owed for a missed week. And there is something about talking into a phone in the dark that people simply do not manage on a video call. Not for the first time, the version that asked least of us turned out to be the one that lasted, which is probably worth remembering the next time I plan something ambitious.

what_lifts_it.point: A fronted 'what has kept it alive' cleft and a 'not for the first time' inversion opener.
'Persevered', 'peculiar quality', 'aggressively unremarkable' — precision rather than rarity.
The close states a general rule about habits instead of summing up the friendship.

annotations.why: Hold the subject open across a clause, then land the answer.

annotations.label: Cleft opening the third bullet
annotations.why: 'What stopped me was…' announces the turn and buys a beat of thinking.

annotations.span: how I'd feel if I came across a photograph of myself asleep
annotations.label: Second conditional inside a thought
annotations.why: Reporting what you imagined keeps the tense honest and adds a structure.

annotations.label: Idiom that concedes a motive
annotations.why: Reuse it any time you want to complicate your own answer.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
This was on the train home one evening last spring. Opposite me a man had fallen asleep in a position no one could have arranged deliberately: head thrown back, mouth open, a half-eaten sandwich still in his hand. I photographed him, which does me no credit whatsoever.

It was destined for a group I share with forty or so people from university, where things of that kind appear daily and vanish by morning. The caption was written. My thumb was hovering.

What pulled me up was the lanyard. He worked somewhere in the city, his name was entirely legible, and it dawned on me that among forty people the odds of somebody recognising him were not small at all. Nor was it much of a leap to imagine finding myself asleep and named on a group I had never joined.

So it went. Was that the right call? On balance yes, though I wouldn't dress it up as principle. A good deal of it was not fancying the role of the man who posts that sort of thing. What has stayed with me is the pause itself, rather than anything I concluded from it. Almost nothing that circulates about strangers involves one, and the more I think about it the less certain I am that the difference between decency and simple cowardice matters half as much as whether anybody stops at all. The photograph was gone in a second; the hesitation is still there.

what_lifts_it.point: Negative inversion with 'nor was it', and a rhetorical question used to open the judgement.
'Pulled me up', 'dawned on me', 'dress it up as' — idiom placed, not exhibited.
The close abstracts into a claim about hesitation rather than defending the decision.

annotations.span: Nor was it much of a leap to imagine finding myself asleep and named
annotations.label: Negative inversion after 'nor'
annotations.why: 'Nor' at the start forces the inversion. Use it once per turn.

annotations.span: a position no one could have arranged deliberately
annotations.label: Modal perfect in a description
annotations.why: 'Could have' lets you evaluate the scene while still describing it.

annotations.span: which does me no credit whatsoever
annotations.label: Formal idiom, self-critical
annotations.why: One phrase concedes fault without a sentence of apology.

annotations.span: though I wouldn't dress it up as principle
annotations.label: Phrasal verb undercutting yourself
annotations.why: 'Dress up as' says presented-as-better-than-it-was in three words.

annotations.span: the less certain I am that the difference between decency and simple cowardice matters half as much as whether anybody stops at all
annotations.label: Ends on a genuine complication
annotations.why: Finishing on an unresolved thought reads as thinking, not as a rehearsed close.
